title: The time is uncertain
hookLine: 'i don't know' feels like failing a test; a weaver's daughter said it to the Buddha, and he praised her
tomorrow: why would anyone call waking up in the morning a wonder?

lines: FOUR QUESTIONS IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
cards: Saying I don't know in class can feel like failing out loud. Now a crowd in the town of Alavi, gathered around the Buddha. A young weaver's daughter slips in late, and he speaks to her, in front of everyone.
Where have you come from? I don't know. Where are you going?
I don't know. Don't you know? I know.
Do you know? I don't know. The crowd mutters.

teach.b: The story is told in the old commentary on the Dhammapada. The Buddha asks her to explain, and she does. Where have I come from?
I don't know which life I came from. Where am I going? I don't know where I'll be born next.
I know that I will die. Do I know?

I don't know when. Every answer was exact. The commentary says she had taken the Buddha's teaching on death to heart when he'd visited before, and kept it up, so his questions landed on someone already listening.
And there's a hard turn, said gently. The commentary says that same day, she died in an accident at her father's loom. She had been right: she didn't know when.

That's the second of Atisha's three roots: the time of death is uncertain. Teachers who hand it down add that a lifespan isn't fixed, that the young can go before the old, and that no calendar has the date.
It isn't there to scare anyone. It works on the sneaky thought under all our postponing: sure, I'll die, but not soon. The weaver's daughter didn't claim to know more than she did.
She held one thing certain and one thing open, and lived between them, listening.
No one knows when. So the kind word, the practice, the visit, doesn't wait for a date.

how: The weaver's daughter is a well-known story in Theravada teaching on mindfulness of death; in Tibetan Buddhism, the uncertainty of the time of death is the second root of the death contemplation taught near the start of the lamrim.

games.q: what does “the time is uncertain” mean?
o: a teacher who isn't sure of his own answers
death is certain, but its hour is unknown
the future is too unclear to make any plans

games.q: her four answers — tap the pairs.
p: i don't know where i'll be born
i know that i will die

s: the crowd was right: she was being rude to the Buddha
the Buddha said well answered; each 'i don't know' was exact.
the second root says no calendar has the date of anyone's death
a lifespan isn't fixed, and the young can go before the old.
uncertain time means you can safely assume it isn't soon
that's the sneaky thought the root works on: sure, i'll die, but not soon.

games.q: the Buddha asks you, in front of a crowd, 'do you know when you'll die?' everyone is listening. what does the weaver's daughter say?
o: 'not for many years, i hope; i'm young and healthy.'
games.why: she held one thing certain, that she would die, and one thing open, when. the Buddha praised her answer.

practice: Listen for one sound around you: a car, the fridge, a bird, a voice in another room. Notice you didn't know it was coming, and you can't say when it will stop. Rest with that sound and the second root together: no one knows when.

wordCard.voice: The time is uncertain: Atisha's second root. Death is sure; its hour isn't, for anyone.

orig.note: Pali: impermanent, not lasting; why no one can know the hour.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: no one knows when, so the kind word doesn't wait for a date. Day sixteen thirty-two, well answered.

sources.ref: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada-atthakatha) on verse 174: the story of the weaver's daughter of Alavi
